newsitem.title: USA: CME pork bellies end limit up after tumultuous day.
newsitem.headline: CME pork bellies end limit up after tumultuous day.

text.p: CME pork belly futures tumbled from early limit gains down to net losses on a wave of profit taking and sell stops before surging back at the close for limit gains. Hog futures followed the trend in bellies and posted net losses before closing strong. Both bellies and hogs posted new contract highs.
Pork bellies closed up the daily 3.000-cent-a-lb limit to up 0.275 cent with May through August locked limit up at the close. May ended at 95.125 and July at 94.675, both new contract highs.
Hog futures ended up 0.600 cent per lb to off 0.050 cent with June up 0.425 at 85.375 cents. June set a new high of 86.600 cents earlier.

Traders said the market was nervous after a recent runup to new highs for the fifth consecutive day and the least little selling or profit taking sparked a sharp down swing. But sellers on the initial break turned buyers at the lows and the ensuing short covering took futures back up the daily limit, they said.
"Strong fundamentals have not gone away," one trade said.
Strong technicals were reinforcing gains linked to rising cash belly prices, light hog slaughter and tight stocks. Export demand was also cited, traders said.
Cash belly prices this week climbed to the highest levels since mid-August.

"Once bellies moved over a top of 90 cents in the futures there wasn't anything in the market to stop it till we get to the dollar mark - there's an old gap we left on weekly charts last summer," said Dale Durchholz, market analyst for AgriVisor Services Inc.
Much of the strength in cash bellies appeared to be coming from export demand as recent high prices were likely slowing domestic interest in bacon, traders said.
Japan announced recently that it was buying U.S. bellies to fill needs following the Taiwan's pork ban.
"The big thing that got that (runup in bellies) going was basically the Japanese news," Durchholz said.

Rand Financials bought May while R.J. O'Brien and Refco bought July and ING bought August, traders said. ABN Chicago Corp and Smith Barney sold August to start the late break but were active buyers on the late advance, sources said.
Pork belly options and 150 unfilled orders in Jly and 90 in August point to higher prices again Friday. July closed synthetically at 95.000 and August at 92.000, they added.
The Taiwan pork ban remained an underlying supportive factor in hog futures as well, but volatility in the pork belly pit influenced trade much of the day, traders said.

The latest reports from Taiwan put 18 percent of that country's hog farms infected with the foot-and-mouth disease with official projections that over 3.54 million of the Island's 14 million hogs have or would be destroyed.
Hogs fell for net losses when pork bellies broke and ran up at the close when bellies again rallied the daily limit. Higher cash hog prices provided some strength, sources said.

Analysts said a decline in the number of market-ready hogs has forced packers to bid higher to ensure slaughter needs were covered. Hog numbers are also seen lower going into the summer based on the last Hogs and Pigs report.

Rand Financials and Rosenthal Collins were on both sides of the market late, traders said. R.J. O'Brien, Prudential Securities, Fimat Futures USA and Dean Witter bought June while Lind-Waldock sold, pit sources said.

In hog options, First Chicago bought July 82 puts and sold July 90 calls while Lind-Waldock bought October 78 and 82 calls early. Commission houses sold puts and bought calls on the late break, pit sources added.
